signature.instructions:
Perform paragraph-level multi-label section classification for CONSORT randomized-trial articles using the supplied `fixed_task_spec` as the controlling specification. Follow its canonical labels, input format, and required JSON output exactly.

Core operating rules
- Return valid JSON only, with no markdown or explanation.
- Include every input paragraph identifier exactly once, in article order.
- Use `pnum` for JSON paragraph objects; use the bracketed paragraph number for plain-text inputs.
- Never reproduce paragraph text.
- Every `sections` array must be non-empty.
- Section membership is paragraph-level, not sentence-level.
- Use global article order and surrounding headings to resolve context, but classify the actual function/content of each paragraph.
- Most paragraphs have one label. Add labels only for distinct, explicit functions actually present in the paragraph. For genuine boundary ambiguity, favor recall modestly: include a plausible additional section when the paragraph clearly contains evidence native to that additional section. Do not broadly add labels merely because nearby sections differ.

General article-structure strategy
1. Identify the title/summary/abstract block, then introduction, methods, results, discussion, and back matter.
2. Classify ordinary section headings with the section they introduce.
3. Classify captions, tables, figures, panels, and isolated headings by their substantive function, not merely their document object type.
4. Treat a paragraph as potentially multi-label when it combines material from different section functions, especially method procedures with reported recruitment/results information.
5. Do not assume all end matter is `other_information`: benchmark conventions can assign transitional “Back matter” and immediately associated material to `discussion` when it remains structurally attached to the discussion. Conversely, substantive acknowledgments, contributors, funding, conflicts, and supplementary-material metadata are usually `other_information`.

Important content-routing rules
- Abstract/title material is usually `title_abstract`, including title, abstract headings, structured abstract headings, and ordinary abstract background/methods/results/conclusion prose.
- However, trial-registration and funding declarations appearing in an abstract are commonly benchmarked as `other_information`, even if they occur in a structured abstract:
  - A registration identifier/declaration such as “Trial registration ISRCTN…” is `other_information`, not also `title_abstract`.
  - An abstract funding heading/value can be `other_information`.
  - There is a known heading/content distinction: an isolated “Trial registration” heading may be `title_abstract` when it belongs to the abstract structure, while the following registry identifier is `other_information`.
- Do not automatically give an abstract paragraph both `title_abstract` and `other_information` merely because it includes a registration statement. In the observed benchmark, the registration/funding content itself takes `other_information` alone.

Methods versus other-information distinctions
- Trial design, recruitment procedures, eligibility, consent procedures, randomization, masking, intervention delivery, outcome assessment, sample-size planning, and statistical analysis are `methods`.
- Ethics approval or consent text embedded in a participant/recruitment procedure is generally `methods` only, not `other_information`, when its operative function is describing how the trial was conducted.
- “Role of the funding source” and its associated statement that the funder/sponsor had no role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation, writing, or publication are `methods` in this benchmark, not `other_information`.
- Do not classify every mention of funding as `other_information`; distinguish a back-matter funding declaration from a methods-section funder-role statement.
- Conversely, standalone funding, conflicts, author contributions, acknowledgments, data sharing, trial registration, protocol availability, citation metadata, and similar declarations in back matter are normally `other_information`.

Methods/results multi-label cases
- Add both `methods` and `results` when a methods-context paragraph explicitly reports completed trial timing, follow-up end dates, recruitment accomplishment, or other observed/reported trial facts in addition to describing the design or procedures.
  - Example pattern: “Between [dates] we conducted the trial … Follow-up ended [date]” can be `methods` + `results`.
- Add `results` to a methods/analysis paragraph when it explicitly reports empirical comparison or observed baseline/result information, rather than only stating planned analysis.
- In rare mixed paragraphs, include `other_information` too if an explicit information/metadata function is present, rather than assuming that a software/database mention alone always qualifies.

Figures, tables, captions, and panels
- Never label a table, figure, or caption `other_information` solely because it is a table/figure/caption.
- Classify trial profile, participant flow, baseline characteristics, outcome tables, adverse-event tables, efficacy/safety figures, Kaplan–Meier curves, endpoint graphics, and their captions as `results`.
- Classify captions describing intervention details, eligibility, randomization, masking, or assessment procedures as `methods` when they genuinely provide those procedural details.
- In this benchmark, an isolated caption “Figure 1 Study design” was labeled `results`; therefore, for minimal figure captions that only name a study-design figure and contain no actual procedural description, prefer `results` rather than `methods`.
- A “Trial profile” figure/caption is `results`.
- Tables titled “Baseline characteristics” or “Results…” are `results`.

Discussion and back-matter benchmark behavior
- Discussion includes interpretation, conclusions, limitations, strengths, applicability, implications, future research, and “what this study adds/what is already known” summaries.
- Isolated discussion headings and panel headings within the discussion inherit `discussion`.
- Be alert to benchmark structural inheritance at the discussion/back-matter boundary. In prior examples, “Back matter,” “List of abbreviations,” “Competing interests,” and “Authors’ contributions” immediately following a discussion were labeled `discussion`, despite their normal semantic association with `other_information`.
- Apply that unusual convention narrowly: when these items are structurally retained in or immediately attached to the article’s discussion section, use `discussion`; when clearly presented as separate, conventional back-matter sections after a distinct back-matter boundary, use `other_information`.
- A standalone “Back matter” heading can therefore be `discussion` when it directly continues the discussion in the source structure, but may be `other_information` when it begins a clearly separate metadata block. Use surrounding hierarchy and sequence.

Avoid these specific recurring mistakes
- Do not add `title_abstract` to a standalone trial-registration identifier.
- Do not add `other_information` to participant/consent procedures merely because ethics committees or approval are mentioned.
- Do not label “Role of the funding source” or its explanatory funder-independence statement as `other_information`; use `methods`.
- Do not classify all final-page items as `other_information` without checking whether the benchmark’s structural context assigns them to `discussion`.
- Do not classify a figure caption as `methods` solely because its title says “Study design”; minimal “Figure … Study design” captions are benchmarked as `results`.
- Do not omit `results` from paragraphs that mix method description with reported recruitment/follow-up dates or observed analyses.

Before returning, verify:
- JSON parses.
- `article_id` exactly matches the provided ID.
- Every and only input pnums appear once.
- Labels use only the canonical labels from `fixed_task_spec`.
- Each paragraph has at least one label.
